4: Microsoft Graph and Entra I D run as separate national cloud deployments, and a script has to call the hosts of the cloud its tenant lives in.

Commercial and Microsoft 365 G C C tenants use the same worldwide hosts: login dot microsoftonline dot com for sign-in and graph dot microsoft dot com for Graph, with the Global environment in Graph PowerShell.
Microsoft's own words are that a G C C environment should continue using the worldwide endpoints.
G C C High and D O D both sign in at login dot microsoftonline dot U S. G C C High's Graph host is graph dot microsoft dot U S, and D O D's is dod dash graph dot microsoft dot U S.
In Graph PowerShell those are the U S Gov and U S Gov D O D environments, and Azure PowerShell and the Azure CLI switch to Azure U S Government.
5: Beyond the hosts, five things change.
The token's scope names the cloud, so app-only tokens for G C C High ask for graph dot microsoft dot U S slash dot default.
The Python azure-identity credential signs in to the public cloud unless you give it the Azure Government authority.
Apps are registered per cloud: an app registered in a commercial tenant can't read a G C C High tenant's data.
Graph Explorer isn't supported on the G C C High, D O D or China endpoints, so a query you proved in Graph Explorer has to be retested against the government endpoint.
And every Graph A P I reference page has a national cloud table; check it before you rely on an A P I in a new cloud.
G C C needs none of this, but it can lack features, which is the Federal Modernization Workbook's Book 10's subject.
6: A scheduled script signs in as itself, not as a person: an app registration and its service principal, with application permissions, using the client credentials flow.
What matters is what the app proves its identity with.

In order of preference, which is design guidance from the sources: a managed identity when the script runs on an Azure resource or an Arc-enabled server, because there's no credential to store or rotate.
Workload identity federation for GitHub Actions, Kubernetes, or any platform that issues its own tokens.
A certificate issued by a certificate authority anywhere else, which Microsoft recommends over a secret.
And a client secret, which you avoid: ScubaGear says application passwords should be blocked.
Graph application permissions need a Privileged Role Administrator.
Plan that approval step: it's the moment someone with privilege decides what the script may read.
7: Graph has two kinds of permission.
Delegated permissions act for a signed-in user and are limited by what that user can do.
Application permissions act as the app, across the whole tenant.
Every A P I reference page lists permissions in order, least privileged first, and you ask for the least one that does the job.
In Graph PowerShell, Find dash Mg Graph Command and Find dash Mg Graph Permission help you find them.
Where a narrower permission exists, use it: enabling and disabling accounts needs User dot Enable Disable Account dot All plus User dot Read dot All, not read-write on all users.
And watch what a narrow permission hides.
Objects you can't fully read still come back, with only an I D and a type.
A null property may mean not permitted, not empty.
The example kit keeps every call and its permission in one file, graph-calls dot jay-son, and a task can make only the calls listed for it.

9: Every Graph script needs the same four patterns.
Collections come back a page at a time: a hundred users by default, up to nine hundred ninety-nine with top, or five hundred when you select sign-in activity.
Follow the next link, unchanged, until it stops appearing.
Over a limit, Graph answers four twenty-nine with a Retry-After header.
Wait that long, because retrying at once keeps counting against you.
A batch takes at most twenty requests, and each one is still throttled on its own, so a batch can succeed while some requests inside it fail.
Follow the next links until you get a delta link, store it, and next time you get only the changes.
And some advanced Entra queries, like count and search, need the ConsistencyLevel eventual header, or they fail or return something different.
10: The limits are layered, and the first one you reach applies.
Every service allows a hundred thirty thousand requests per ten seconds per app, across all tenants.

Entra I D objects, like users, groups and applications, use cost-based resource units instead: thirty-five hundred, five thousand or eight thousand per ten seconds per app and tenant, depending on the tenant's size.
A request's cost changes with what you ask for.
Select lowers it by one, expand raises it by one, and a top under twenty lowers it by one.
Listing a group's transitive members costs five, against three for direct members.
And a background job, like an evidence collector, can send a low throttle priority.
Microsoft recommends high priority only for requests a user started.

13: Most on this path run a Microsoft 365 G C C tenant with commercial Azure.
Their scripts are often older than the current tools: AzureAD cmdlets, a client secret in a scheduled task, a host name written into the code.
Some run G C C High.
For what this module relies on: in G C C High and D O D, the app is registered in the government cloud itself, and Graph Explorer isn't supported.

The interim paths: rewrite retired-module scripts on Graph PowerShell, use a certificate on premises until the server is on Arc, and treat a G C C High move as a configuration change.
